name: The world as Will
plain_explanation: Schopenhauer argues that what appears to us, in perception, as our own body is really, in its inner nature, our will; and since space and time (which are what make things separate and many) belong only to appearance and not to ultimate reality, this will cannot really be many separate individual wills -- it must be a single, timeless, universal Will underlying the whole of nature, animate and inanimate alike.
precise_definition: Schopenhauer's central metaphysical claim, developed from Kant: the 'thing-in-itself' (retained, unlike in Fichte and Hegel) is identical with Will; since time and space (Kant's 'principle of individuation') belong only to phenomena, the thing-in-itself/Will cannot be plural or composed of discrete acts of will, and is therefore one, timeless, and identical with the will of the whole universe, of which individual selfhood is merely an illusion of subjective, spatio-temporal perception.
why_it_mattered: It is the foundation of Schopenhauer's whole system, and represents, in Russell's assessment, a more defensible development of certain genuine strands in Kant (the connection of the moral law and the thing-in-itself to volition) than most Kantians acknowledged.
historical_origin: The World as Will and Idea (1818).
examples: Schopenhauer's claim that 'what appears to perception as my body is really my will'
The kept poodle named 'Atma' (world-soul), reflecting Schopenhauer's Hindu-influenced monism
competing_positions: Fichte's and Hegel's abandonment of the thing-in-itself, making knowledge (not will) metaphysically fundamental
Spinoza's pantheism, which Schopenhauer's cosmic-will doctrine initially resembles but then diverges from sharply via pessimism
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly inaugurates the 'primacy of will' tradition Russell traces through Nietzsche, Bergson, James, and Dewey.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Draws explicitly on Hindu and Buddhist metaphysics (the veil of Maya, the illusion of individuation).
